set.statement: Randomized evidence on antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, as identified by a systematic review and network meta-analysis with searches to June 2020, consists of six small, short (21 to 42 days), single-site trials with 395 participants in Thailand, Iran and China, mostly inpatients and mostly men, each comparing two of six antipsychotics (aripiprazole, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone extended-release, quetiapine, risperidone); none had a placebo or no-medication arm, and two are titled as trials in amphetamine psychosis. Each trial reported no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms, and the trials were too small to show that the drugs work equally well. Chaining the trials through their shared drugs, the network meta-analysis estimated that olanzapine (standardized mean difference −1.09, 95% CI −1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine (−0.86, −1.61 to −0.11) reduced symptoms more than risperidone and that aripiprazole did worse than four of the other drugs; these are indirect estimates only, rated low certainty by the authors because data came partly from open-label trials and the trials differ in participants and design, and both advantages over risperidone rest on one open-label trial of haloperidol against risperidone with 44 participants. Dropout did not differ, but its intervals were too wide to be informative. Because no trial had a placebo arm, these trials cannot show whether antipsychotics speed recovery beyond what abstinence alone achieves; the one placebo-controlled trial the review found, of aripiprazole in people whose psychotic symptoms had already subsided, was excluded. Side effects were not pooled; as narrative reviews describe it, the one trial included in a 2009 Cochrane review found fewer extrapyramidal side effects on olanzapine than on haloperidol. Two narrative reviews state that acute psychosis usually resolves with abstinence alone, citing early studies of amphetamine psychosis published between 1958 and 1980 or an online clinical reference entry. How often psychosis persists after stopping is described in section 9.
set.plain: A 2021 review found only six small trials, about 400 people in all, testing medicines for meth psychosis, always one medicine against another, never against a dummy pill. No trial found a clear difference between its two medicines; indirect comparisons favouring some medicines are uncertain. None of these trials tested whether the medicines help more than stopping meth alone.
set.magnitude: Six head-to-head randomized trials (searches to June 2020), 395 participants, 42 to 120 per trial, 21 to 42 days; no placebo arm. Network estimates against risperidone, main symptoms (SMD): olanzapine −1.09 (−1.89 to −0.28) and quetiapine −0.86 (−1.61 to −0.11), indirect only; haloperidol −0.60 (−1.20 to 0.01), paliperidone extended-release −0.33 (−0.69 to 0.03) and aripiprazole 0.27 (−0.13 to 0.68), direct. Aripiprazole against olanzapine 1.36 (0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine 1.13 (0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol 0.87 (0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release 0.60 (0.06 to 1.14), indirect. No direct comparison significant. Dropout odds ratios against risperidone 0.18 to 2.77, every interval including 1. Authors' GRADE: low or very low for every estimate.
set.grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence, now read through a systematic review and network meta-analysis (Srisurapanont et al., 2021; AMSTAR 2 low confidence on the first reading), so the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews; the six trial reports themselves have not been read. Starts high. Risk of bias −1: two of the six trials were open-label (high risk in two domains) and allocation concealment was unclear in four; both indirect advantages over risperidone, and three of the four against aripiprazole, are chained through the open-label haloperidol–risperidone pilot trial (44 participants). Indirectness −1: the network is a chain without a closed loop, so every indirect estimate rests on transitivity, which the authors themselves doubt (participants and designs differ); two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis; and active-comparator trials cannot address benefit beyond abstinence, the claim's open question. Imprecision −2: 42 to 120 participants per trial, every direct comparison's interval includes no difference, and dropout odds ratios have intervals as wide as 0.00 to 218. Publication bias not assessable with six trials (funnel plots only); not downgraded, noted. Very low. Status replicated: six trials, from at least five independent groups (the two Chinese trials share authors), each reported no significant difference between its two drugs; the network's indirect differences come from one analysis and are not replicated. The olanzapine–haloperidol trial (Leelahanaj et al., 2005), probably the trial the narrative reviews describe as the 2009 Cochrane review's single trial with 58 participants, is listed in the network meta-analysis with 56 (29 and 27). Not yet read (built-in browser unavailable on 2026-10-17): the systematic reviews of Fluyau et al. (2019) and Hall et al. (2026), and the 24-month randomized trial of aripiprazole or paliperidone against treatment as usual (Chung et al., 2026), which the currency check of 2026-10-16 identifies as bearing on benefit beyond usual care.
set.population: Adults with methamphetamine psychosis (two trials are titled as amphetamine psychosis), mostly inpatients and men, in trials in Thailand, Iran and China
set.outcome: Severity of psychotic symptoms after 3 to 6 weeks; dropout; side effects (narrative reviews only)

evidence_add.extracted: Searches to 15 June 2020 without language limits found six randomized trials, 395 participants with methamphetamine psychosis, all comparing two antipsychotics head to head and none with a placebo arm: aripiprazole vs risperidone (2 trials), olanzapine vs haloperidol, haloperidol vs quetiapine, haloperidol vs risperidone and paliperidone extended-release vs risperidone (1 each). Arms: risperidone 129, haloperidol 93, aripiprazole 48, paliperidone extended-release 60, quetiapine 36, olanzapine 29. Trials lasted 21 to 42 days, were single-site (two each in Thailand, Iran and China; five inpatient, one outpatient), and two are titled as trials in amphetamine psychosis (Leelahanaj 2005; Farnia 2014). Editors' sums from Table 1: 42 to 120 participants per trial; the olanzapine–haloperidol trial has 29 and 27, 56 in all.

The authors' GRADE started high and downgraded every estimate one level for indirectness (intransitivity: participants and designs varied across trials), comparisons using data from the open-label trials for risk of bias, and estimates whose interval included no difference for imprecision: all main-symptom estimates low or very low.

evidence_add.extracted: No included trial had a placebo arm, which the discussion lists among the limitations; the one placebo-controlled trial found (Sulaiman 2013, aripiprazole for 8 weeks) was excluded because its participants had recovered from psychotic symptoms (Fig. 1: mean PANSS total 51.6, less than mildly psychotic). Dropout did not differ significantly, with odds ratios against risperidone from 0.18 (olanzapine, 95% CI 0.00 to 50.14) to 2.77 (aripiprazole, 0.32 to 23.95) and I² 72.5%; the values in Figs. 1 and 3C were read from the images.

change: First reader 12 (2026-10-17), currency update: the claim now rests on a systematic review and network meta-analysis read in full (Srisurapanont et al., 2021; six head-to-head trials, 395 participants, searches to June 2020) and no longer only on narrative reviews (METHODS §6.3), so it leaves draft for metadata-verified. Statement, plain text, magnitude, population and outcome rewritten from the review: the trial inventory, each trial's non-significant result, the low-certainty indirect network estimates and their dependence on one open-label trial, the excluded placebo-controlled trial, and the narrative reviews' side-effect and abstinence remarks kept with their sources. Status single study → replicated (six trials in the same direction). GRADE levels unchanged (very low), reasons rewritten. Six anchors added (located). Fluyau 2019, Hall 2026 and Chung 2026 not yet read (browser unavailable).

set.statement: In a systematic review of studies of methamphetamine-associated psychosis to March 2018, mostly of hospital patients and without appraisal of study quality, 27 studies reported the share of participants still psychotic more than a month after stopping use: the median study reported 25%, ranging from none in six laboratory studies in which volunteers were given the drug (symptoms resolved within 12 hours to 7 days) to 96%, with a median of 40% in longitudinal studies; Japanese studies reported more persistence (median 44%) than studies elsewhere (12%), which the review's authors attribute to the ICD rule allowing psychosis to last up to 6 months before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed. Second-hand reports of hospital series add 27% and 17% still psychotic beyond one and three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment in 104 Japanese inpatients (cited by the systematic review); 16% and 17% after 1 and 3 months of abstinence in two reports from one Taiwanese research group, probably on one sample (a systematic review combines them as one study population of 445), with the denominator not explained and conflicting statements on family history in the narrative review that quotes them; and 10–28% beyond 6 months (narrative reviews). Later schizophrenia diagnoses ranged from 5% (China, second-hand) to about 39% in a Thai cohort of more than 1,000 people after a first hospitalization, a figure three reviews give differently (38.8% at 5 years; nearly 40% within 6 years; and, if the systematic review's study of 1,116 people after a first hospitalization is the same cohort, 33–38% after 6–7 years together with a study of 28 people); the systematic review gives 16% within 16 years for a Finnish register study of 825 people, and a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. These figures cannot show whether methamphetamine caused a lasting illness or revealed an existing vulnerability, whether some first episodes were primary psychoses attributed to drug use, or whether some later diagnoses relabel a persistent methamphetamine psychosis, since one review notes that diagnostic rules call for a primary psychotic diagnosis once psychosis persists. Recurrence with renewed use is common in clinical series, and in one follow-up positive symptoms rose in former patients who resumed use; Japanese researchers, as one review reports, describe spontaneous relapses after remission, which stressful situations seem to trigger in susceptible people. None of these figures has been checked in the primary studies, and a 2020 meta-analysis of transition to schizophrenia has not yet been read.
set.plain: Across 27 studies of meth-related psychosis, mostly in hospital patients, the typical study found 1 in 4 people still had symptoms over a month after stopping; studies ranged from none to almost all. About 1 in 20 to 2 in 5 were later diagnosed with schizophrenia, which does not show meth caused it. Psychosis often returns with renewed use.
set.magnitude: Systematic review, 27 studies with duration data: median 25% still psychotic beyond one month (laboratory studies 0%; longitudinal studies median 40%, range 14–96%; Japanese studies median 44%, range 18–96%, against 12%, range 0–39%, elsewhere; t = 4.79, p = .0001); case reports 2 of 24. Later schizophrenia diagnosis: 33–38% after 6–7 years (two studies, 1116 and 28 people); 16% within 16 years (825 people). Second-hand in narrative reviews: 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months (one research group, probably one sample); beyond 6 months 10–28%; later schizophrenia 5.0% (China) to 38.8% at 5 years (Thailand; nearly 40% within 6 years in another review); 19.1–30% in register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis. Japanese inpatient series cited by the systematic review: 27% beyond one month, 17% beyond three months (n=104). No pooled estimate or interval.
set.grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim (base rates of persistence and of later diagnosis); observational, starts low. The claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews: a systematic review read in full (Voce et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low on the first reading) now supports the persistence and transition figures, although it reports them second-hand from primary studies it did not appraise, as unweighted medians without intervals. Risk of bias −1: mostly hospital samples, abstinence not verified, antipsychotic treatment and polydrug use not accounted for, and a median that includes six laboratory studies in which persistence was impossible by design. Inconsistency −1: persistence ranges from 0% to 96% across studies, partly explained by diagnostic rules (median 44% in Japanese studies, which mostly used ICD-10, against 12% elsewhere); later schizophrenia diagnosis ranges from 5% to about 39%, the Thai figure and its follow-up are reported differently by three reviews, and the Finnish register study appears as 16% within 16 years in the systematic review while a narrative review gives 19–30% for register studies. Very low. Not yet read (built-in browser unavailable on 2026-10-17): the 2020 meta-analysis of transition from substance-induced psychoses to schizophrenia (Murrie et al.), which should replace the second-hand transition figures, and the register cohorts the currency check of 2026-10-16 lists.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Duration of symptoms, 1st paragraph
evidence_add.extracted: Twenty-seven studies (12 case-control, 5 cross-sectional, 4 longitudinal, 6 laboratory) reported the share of participants with psychotic symptoms more than one month after stopping use: median 25%; no persistence in the 6 laboratory studies, where symptoms abated within 12 hours to 7 days of the last dose; longitudinal studies median 40% (range 14–96%). Case reports: 2 of 24 persisted beyond one month (8%).

evidence_add.locator: Results › Duration of symptoms, 2nd paragraph (p. 6); Discussion › Duration of psychotic symptoms, 1st paragraph (pp. 7–8)
evidence_add.extracted: Japanese studies (k = 11, 41% of those with duration data) reported a median of 44% persisting (range 18–96%) against 12% (range 0–39%) in fourteen studies from the USA, Australia, Canada, Iran and elsewhere in Asia (t = 4.79, p = .0001); Japanese studies more often used ICD-10 (35%) than DSM-IV (25%), the others DSM-IV (42%) more than ICD-10 (6%). The discussion attributes the excess to the ICD classification, under which psychosis can persist up to 6 months after intoxication before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Longitudinal changes in symptom profile, 2nd paragraph
evidence_add.extracted: Three longitudinal studies reported later schizophrenia diagnoses: 33–38% re-diagnosed after 6–7 years in two (Kittirattanapaiboon et al., 2010, 1116 people; Medhus et al., 2015, 28 people) and 16% within 16 years in a study of 825 patients (Niemi-Pynttäri et al., 2013). The review writes these sample sizes with k, elsewhere its symbol for numbers of studies.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Longitudinal changes in symptom profile, 1st paragraph
evidence_add.extracted: Four longitudinal studies tracked symptoms: positive symptoms fell in three and were stable in one, negative symptoms were stable in three and rose in one (Tomiyama 1990, hospitalized patients on antipsychotics); in a three-month follow-up (Javadian et al., 2016), positive symptoms rose in former patients who resumed methamphetamine use.

evidence_add.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph
evidence_add.extracted: Of 104 psychiatric inpatients with amphetamine delusional disorder who did not meet criteria for schizophrenia (Iwanami et al., 1994, a Japanese hospital series by its title in the reference list), 27% had symptoms beyond one month and 17% beyond three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment.

evidence_add.locator: Results › Participant demographics (p. 4); Discussion › Limitations of the reviewed studies, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 8); Limitations of the current review (p. 9)
evidence_add.extracted: Seventy-two percent of the review's studies recruited hospital in- or outpatients. The authors state that many included studies did not adjust for polydrug use, frequency and duration of use or antipsychotic medication, that no study examined duration in community samples, and that their present-or-absent coding cannot give prevalence and studies were aggregated without weighting for quality or size; no quality appraisal was made.

change: First reader 12 (2026-10-17), currency update: a systematic review read in full (Voce et al., 2019) now supports the persistence and transition figures, so the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS §6.3) and leaves draft for metadata-verified. Statement, plain text and magnitude now lead with the review's figures (27 studies: median 25% still psychotic beyond one month, range 0–96%; Japanese 44% vs 12% elsewhere; later schizophrenia 33–38% after 6–7 years and 16% within 16 years) and keep the narrative reviews' second-hand figures with their caveats, adding a Japanese inpatient series and a follow-up of renewed use. GRADE levels unchanged (very low), reasons rewritten. Six anchors added (located). Murrie 2020 not yet read (browser unavailable).

set.statement: In a meta-analysis of 12 observational studies to December 2022 (624 people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis and 527 with schizophrenia or a related disorder, mostly treated outpatients described as stable; antipsychotic doses reported in six studies), negative symptoms were less severe in methamphetamine psychosis (standardized mean difference −0.35, 95% CI −0.54 to −0.16; I² 54%; −0.44, −0.82 to −0.07, in studies rated at lower risk of bias), a small-to-moderate difference, significant in 5 of the 12 studies; pooled from three studies, neither diminished expression nor amotivation differed significantly. Positive symptoms did not differ significantly (reported −0.01, −0.13 to 0.11, with no heterogeneity), but that pooled result cannot be reproduced from the review's own table of study means, which gives an imprecise and very heterogeneous comparison (editors' recalculation −0.29, −0.67 to 0.10; I² 89%), so the evidence shows no significant difference rather than similarity. The pooled groups mix acute and persistent psychosis and current and past methamphetamine use; at least one comparison group with a primary psychotic disorder also used methamphetamine, two of the studies, from one research group, probably share participants, and the designs are cross-sectional. As reported in one narrative review of 12 direct comparisons (figures second-hand; at least three of its studies are also in the meta-analysis), more visual and tactile hallucinations in methamphetamine psychosis were found in one comparison of persistent psychosis (about 53 people per group), and a second comparison, of lifetime symptoms in 284 people who all had methamphetamine dependence, is reported in opposite directions in the review's table and text; in one comparison of acute psychosis (33 vs 69 people), voices conversing were more frequent in methamphetamine psychosis (48.5% vs 20.3%) and thought broadcasting in schizophrenia (42% vs 24%, significant only after adjusting for age). In one Taiwanese study, psychosis persisting more than a month into abstinence was comparable to schizophrenia on positive symptoms and on cognitive tests, while people whose psychosis had resolved within a month (abstinent for an average of 9 weeks when assessed) scored lower on positive symptoms and performed like people who used methamphetamine without psychosis. The narrative review's authors conclude that acute methamphetamine psychosis may be clinically distinguishable from schizophrenia while persistent psychosis appears similar, except for more pronounced negative symptoms in schizophrenia; the review reports no study validating any symptom for telling the two apart, and its evidence on thought disorder is mixed and, by its authors' account, indirect and inconclusive.
set.plain: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike. In 12 small studies pooled together, hallucinations and delusions were not clearly different in strength, though this result is less certain than reported. 'Negative' symptoms, such as flatness and withdrawal, were somewhat milder in meth psychosis. No symptom has been shown to reliably tell the two apart.
set.magnitude: Meta-analysis, 12 studies, 624 vs 527 people: negative symptoms SMD −0.35 (−0.54 to −0.16), I² 54%; studies with Newcastle–Ottawa scores above 5: −0.44 (−0.82 to −0.07); without the outlying study: −0.254 (−0.37 to −0.13). Positive symptoms −0.01 (−0.13 to 0.11), I² 0%, as reported; editors' recalculation from the review's Table 1: −0.29 (−0.67 to 0.10), I² 89%. Depressive symptoms (6 studies): −0.01 (−0.41 to 0.39), I² 83%. Narrative review (12 direct comparisons, 1990–2017, figures second-hand): no effect sizes; negative symptoms milder in methamphetamine psychosis in 4 studies, no significant difference in 4; persistent methamphetamine psychosis (n=56) comparable to schizophrenia (n=54) on BPRS total and positive scores and on cognitive tests; the acute group (n=50) had been abstinent for an average of 9 weeks when assessed (Chen et al., 2015, as described in the review).
set.grade.reasoning: Observational comparisons of diagnostic groups; start low. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review: a systematic review and meta-analysis read in full (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024; AMSTAR 2 critically low on the first reading) pools 12 studies, so the severity comparisons are no longer second-hand; the narrative review's study-level descriptions remain second-hand. Risk of bias −1: cross-sectional comparisons of treated patients, with acute and persistent psychosis and current and past use mixed, at least one comparison group using methamphetamine, two studies from one group probably sharing participants, and the meta-analysis's input values for positive symptoms not reproducible from its own table. Inconsistency −1: negative symptoms I² 54% with 5 of 12 studies significant; positive symptoms very heterogeneous on recalculation (I² 89%) although reported as homogeneous; the narrative review's table and text disagree on hallucination modalities in one study. Imprecision not downgraded separately (already very low), although the recalculated positive-symptom interval (−0.67 to 0.10) includes both no difference and a moderate one. Very low. Overlap: at least three primary studies (Chen 2015, Srisurapanont 2011, Wang 2016) are in both the meta-analysis and the narrative review, which therefore do not count as independent replication.

Restricted to studies with Newcastle–Ottawa scores above 5: −0.44 (−0.82 to −0.07, p = 0.04); leaving out the outlier: −0.254 (−0.37 to −0.13), I² 58.0%.

change: First reader 12 (2026-10-17), currency update: a systematic review and meta-analysis read in full (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024; 12 studies, 624 vs 527 people) now carries the severity comparisons, so the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3) and leaves draft for metadata-verified. Negative symptoms milder in methamphetamine psychosis (SMD −0.35, −0.54 to −0.16); the reported positive-symptom null (−0.01) cannot be reproduced from the review's own Table 1 (editors' recalculation −0.29, −0.67 to 0.10, I² 89%) and is stated as no significant difference, not similarity; mixed and partly ineligible groups and probable double counting stated. The narrative review's study-level findings kept, shortened, as second-hand. GRADE levels unchanged (very low), reasons rewritten. Five anchors added (located).

set.plain: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about two and a half times the odds of psychosis, allowing for some other differences. A study following about 1,000 New Zealanders from birth found any use went with slightly more psychotic symptoms, mostly in people who had used weekly. Neither settles which came first.
set.population: Mostly treatment, psychiatric, emergency and criminal-justice samples and samples of people who use drugs; the unadjusted estimates also include a population-wide hospital-admissions cohort and a sample of dance-venue patrons; one general-population birth cohort (New Zealand) gives within-cohort estimates

replace: Most studies cannot show whether use preceded psychosis.

Most studies cannot show whether use preceded psychosis. In a general-population birth cohort in Christchurch, New Zealand (962 to 1,025 people at each of five interviews from age 18 to 35), use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants in a period went with reporting at least one psychotic symptom in the same period: odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.55–2.30) unadjusted and 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for childhood and family factors and for concurrent cannabis use, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and life stress; the outcome was self-reported psychotic experiences on checklist and interview items (35–42% of the cohort reported at least one in each period to age 25), not diagnosed psychosis, and use and symptoms were reported for the same periods, so this cohort cannot show which came first either. The higher odds were concentrated in the 5% who had ever used at least weekly (2.85, 1.21–6.69, adjusted for childhood and family factors only; about 1.3 and not statistically significant for less frequent use).

No absolute risks reported. General-population birth cohort (New Zealand): any use in a period, OR 1.33 (1.03–1.72) after adjustment for fixed and time-varying factors (unadjusted 1.88, 1.55–2.30); ever at least weekly use 2.85 (1.21–6.69), adjusted for fixed factors only; population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2–14.7%) if causal.
it is not in the adjusted use-disorder estimate on which this claim rests.

it is not in the adjusted use-disorder estimate on which this claim rests. Boden et al. (2023), a general-population birth cohort read in full (ROBINS-E high on the first reading, from concerns in several domains), agrees in direction and is smaller after fuller adjustment (any use, OR 1.33, 1.03–1.72, after adjusting for concurrent cannabis use and other time-varying factors; 1.88 unadjusted), which fits the meta-analysis authors' view that unadjusted estimates are inflated; it is not counted as inconsistency, because exposure (any use rather than use disorder), population and outcome (self-reported psychotic experiences) differ. Not upgraded for dose–response: its gradient (2.85 for ever at least weekly use against about 1.3, not significant, for less frequent use) is adjusted only for fixed confounders. It is an independent sample, though it shares an author with McKetin et al. (2013) and the meta-analysis. Huang et al. evidence_add.extracted: Use and symptoms were self-reported for the same period at each interview: use of methamphetamine or other amphetamine-type stimulants (the question named speed, P and ice), and psychotic symptom items from the SCL-90 at ages 18 to 25 (past month) or the Diagnostic Interview Schedule at 30 and 35 (since the previous assessment); 35.2%, 41.8% and 36.4% reported at least one symptom in the periods to age 25; the authors note that some SCL-90 items arguably do not capture genuine psychotic experiences.

evidence_add.extracted: E-value 1.571 (confidence limit 1.11) for unmeasured confounding; population attributable fraction 8.0% (2.2%–14.7%), assuming causality. The authors conclude that methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for psychosis in the general population, on self-reported symptoms reported for the same periods as use.
